lesson.title: Tables, keys and types
lesson.subtitle: How apps store data: primary keys, foreign keys and a schema

video.title: Tables, keys and types
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — the computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Icon cards: A like; Millions a second; A database. Mr Joseph beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Every time you like a photo, an app saves who liked it, which photo, and when. Millions of times a second, for millions of people. Not in a spreadsheet!

scenes.visual: Paper-grey title card: the Darsi mark, the course name and the lesson title with the Data engineering track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark scales in with a small overshoot; the title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: how apps store data in databases, with tables, keys and types.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Many users at once; A type for each column; Rules at the door; Each fact stored once.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: What a database gives an app
scenes.narration: A database keeps the tables for an app. Many users read and write at once, safely. Every column has a type, and rules stop bad data at the door. And every fact is stored once.

scenes.visual: Two columns: “Bad keys” (Names; Birthdays) and “A good key” (An id given once).
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: A primary key: one row, always
scenes.narration: Each table has a primary key: a column whose value is different in every row, like a user id. Names and birthdays make bad keys, because two people can share them.

scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Tables link with foreign keys. A likes table holds a user id and a photo id. Each one points to a row in another table.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: CREATE TABLE likes ( … Caption: One like per user, per photo
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: A schema: the shape of the data
scenes.narration: Designing those tables is called a schema: the tables, their columns and types, and how they link. A good schema stores each fact in exactly one place.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Which column makes the best primary key for a school's pupils?

scenes.visual: Icon cards: Pupil number; Names repeat; So do birthdays.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: A pupil number, given once and never reused. Names and birthdays repeat, and names change spelling.

scenes.visual: Code typed out on a card: SELECT name, class … Caption: Columns, a table, the rows you want
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Then you ask questions in SQL. SELECT picks the columns, FROM the table, and WHERE the rows. It works the same on twelve rows or twelve million.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: Stored twice: copies drift; One row changed, five missed; Stored once: one story.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Store a fact twice and the copies drift apart. Change a teacher's phone in one row, miss five others, and the database tells two stories.

scenes.visual: Icon cards joined by arrows: One table: 32; Two: 8; Three: 0.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: one fact, one place
scenes.narration: In the app, split a wide school table into two, then three. The repeated facts fall from thirty-two to eight to zero. Then try a hurried change on each design.

scenes.visual: Quiz card: the question with its answer options.
scenes.animation: Answer cards drop in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Why store the class teacher's name in a classes table, and not in every pupil's row?

scenes.visual: Summary card: Primary key: one row; Foreign keys link tables; Each fact stored once. Takeaway bar: Design the tables first; the questions come easily.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: So a change happens in one place, and every row agrees. Remember: a primary key picks out one row. Foreign keys link tables. And a good schema stores each fact once.

scenes.visual: Rows of icon and text: An app you use; Sketch its tables and keys; Which tables link?. Mr Joseph beside it.
scenes.animation: Each item arrives as it is said.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: pick an app you use, like a messaging app. Sketch its tables: what is a row in each, and what's the key? Which tables link?

checkpoints.prompt: Which column makes the best primary key for a school's pupils?

options.text: A pupil number the school gives once

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a number given once and never reused picks out exactly one pupil.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — names and birthdays can be shared by two pupils. A primary key must be different in every row.

checkpoints.prompt: Why store the class teacher's name in a classes table, not in every pupil's row?

options.text: So a change happens in one place

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — stored once, it's changed once, and every pupil's row stays right through the link.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the point is one fact in one place: change it once, and every row agrees.
